source_refs.note: Practice long questions written from Chapter 14 (PDF 18-44, printed 15-41); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 14 (Simple Harmonic Motion), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define vibration, amplitude, time period, frequency and angular frequency. Starting from the definition of angular frequency, show that ω = 2π/T = 2πf. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Vibration: one complete round trip (cycle) of a vibrating body about its mean position, e.g. motion of a pendulum bob from A to B and back to A.

Amplitude (x₀): the magnitude of the maximum displacement of the vibrating body on either side of its mean position (OA = OB = x₀).

Time period (T): the time taken to complete one vibration. SI unit: second (s).

Frequency (f): the number of vibrations completed in one second: f = n/t = 1/T. Unit: hertz (Hz), one oscillation per second; dimension [T⁻¹].

Angular frequency (ω): angular displacement per unit time:
ω = θ/t
For one revolution θ = 2π radian and t = T (time period), so
ω = 2π/T
As f = 1/T, therefore
ω = 2πf
and T = 1/f = 2π/ω. SI unit of ω: rad s⁻¹; dimension [T⁻¹].

book_ref.quote: Time period in terms of frequency f and angular frequency ω is expressed as:

blocks.prompt: 2 A vibrating body completes 45 vibrations in 18 s. Find (i) its frequency (ii) its time period (iii) its angular frequency. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Frequency is vibrations per second; T is its reciprocal; ω = 2πf.

book_ref.quote: Frequency is defined as the number of vibrations or oscillations (n) completed by the vibrating body in one second

blocks.final_answer: f = 2.5 Hz, T = 0.4 s, ω ≈ 15.7 rad s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 3 State the conditions necessary for simple harmonic motion. Using Hooke's law and Newton's second law, show that a body attached to a spring on a smooth horizontal surface has an acceleration directly proportional to its displacement and directed towards the mean position. What role does inertia play? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Conditions for S.H.M (14.2):
• The restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position.
• Force and displacement follow Hooke's law, F = −kx.
• The acceleration is proportional to the displacement, a ∝ −x; the negative sign shows it is directed towards the mean position.

Mass-spring system: A body of mass m is attached to a spring of constant k on a smooth horizontal surface; O is the mean position (Fig. 14.2). A force F displaces it from O to A through x. By Hooke's law:
F ∝ x, or F = kx ... (14.1)
The spring exerts an elastic restoring force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction:
F = −kx ... (14.2)
By Newton's second law:
F = ma ... (14.3)
Comparing (14.2) and (14.3):
ma = −kx, or a = −(k/m)x ... (14.4)
k/m is constant, so a = −(constant)x, i.e. a ∝ −x.
This is the mathematical form of S.H.M: acceleration is directly proportional to displacement and, because of the negative sign, always directed towards the mean position.

Role of inertia: When released, the body moves towards O. At O the force is zero, but the body crosses O due to inertia, reaches B and compresses the spring, then returns; so it keeps oscillating between A and B. The restoring force itself depends only on displacement, not on inertia.

book_ref.quote: Consider a body of mass 'm' attached with a spring of spring constant 'k' lying on smooth horizontal surface

blocks.prompt: 4 A 0.3 kg body is attached to a spring of constant 120 N m⁻¹ on a smooth horizontal surface. It is pulled 5 cm to the right and released. Find the restoring force and the acceleration of the body at the moment of release. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use F = −kx for the force, then a = F/m = −(k/m)x; the sign gives the direction.

book_ref.quote: The negative sign shows that acceleration and displacement are always in opposite direction

steps: The negative signs show that force and acceleration point to the left, towards the mean position.
blocks.final_answer: F = 6 N and a = 20 m s⁻², both towards the mean position

blocks.prompt: 5 By comparing the acceleration of a mass-spring system with a = −ω²x, obtain expressions for its angular frequency, frequency and time period. Explain how the time period changes with the mass and with the stiffness of the spring, and name some real-world uses of S.H.M. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
For a mass-spring system (Eq. 14.4):
a = −(k/m)x
For any S.H.M (Eq. 14.8):
a = −ω²x
Comparing:
ω² = k/m, or ω = √(k/m)
Frequency: as ω = 2πf,
f = ω/2π = (1/2π)√(k/m)
Time period: T is the reciprocal of f,
T = 1/f = 2π√(m/k)

Dependence:
• T ∝ √m: a heavier mass gives a longer period (four times the mass, twice the period).
• T ∝ 1/√k: a stiffer spring (larger k) gives a shorter period and a higher frequency.
• T does not depend on the amplitude.

Real-world uses of the S.H.M principle: pendulum clocks, musical instruments and vehicle suspension systems.

book_ref.quote: T is the reciprocal of f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so m/k comes under the root

blocks.prompt: 6 A 0.6 kg mass oscillates on a spring of constant 150 N m⁻¹. Find (i) its angular frequency (ii) frequency (iii) time period. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ω = √(k/m) first; then f = ω/2π and T = 1/f.

book_ref.quote: The last line should read T = 1/f = 2π√(m/k)

blocks.prompt: 7 Resolve the weight of the bob of a simple pendulum at its extreme position and identify the restoring force. Using the small-angle approximation (support it from Table 14.1), show that the bob executes S.H.M, and derive its frequency and time period. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A simple pendulum is a small heavy bob of mass m suspended from a rigid support by a light inextensible string of length ℓ.

Forces: At extreme position P the weight mg makes angle θ with the string (Fig. 14.3 b). Its components are mg cosθ along the string and mg sinθ perpendicular to it. There is no motion along the string, so mg cosθ is cancelled by the tension T. The component mg sinθ is the restoring force towards the mean position:
F = −mg sinθ
By Newton's second law F = ma, so
ma = −mg sinθ, a = −g sinθ ... (14.5)

Small angle: For small angles sinθ ≈ θ (θ in radians). Table 14.1 shows this: e.g. 5° = 0.0873 rad and sin 5° = 0.0872. So
a = −gθ ... (14.6)
With θ = S/ℓ (S = arc length): a = −(g/ℓ)S. For a small angle (about 10° or less) x ≈ S, so
a = −(g/ℓ)x ... (14.7)
For fixed ℓ and g, g/ℓ is constant: a ∝ −x. Hence the motion of a simple pendulum is S.H.M.

Frequency and period: Comparing with a = −ω²x (14.8):
ω² = g/ℓ, ω = √(g/ℓ) ... (14.9)
As ω = 2πf: f = (1/2π)√(g/ℓ)
T = 1/f = 2π√(ℓ/g) ... (14.10)
T is directly proportional to √ℓ, inversely proportional to √g, and independent of the mass of the bob and of the (small) amplitude.

book_ref.quote: We can resolve weight into its rectangular components.

blocks.prompt: 8 A simple pendulum is 1.6 m long. Taking g = 9.8 m s⁻², find its (i) angular frequency (ii) time period (iii) frequency. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use ω = √(g/ℓ), then T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T.

book_ref.quote: The above expression shows that the time period of simple pendulum is directly proportional to the square root

blocks.prompt: 9 Describe how a simple pendulum is used to determine the acceleration due to gravity at a place. Why should the amplitude be kept small? What is a second pendulum, and would the same pendulum keep the same period on the Moon? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Method: The time period of a simple pendulum is
T = 2π√(ℓ/g) ... (14.10)
Squaring: T² = 4π²ℓ/g, so
g = 4π²ℓ/T²
Measure the length ℓ of the pendulum. Set it into motion with a small amplitude and measure the time period T with a stopwatch (for accuracy, time several vibrations and divide by their number). Substitute ℓ and T to find g at that location.

Why a small amplitude: The result T = 2π√(ℓ/g) uses sinθ ≈ θ and x ≈ arc S, which hold only for small angles (about 10° or less). Only then is a ∝ −x and the motion S.H.M with this period.

Second pendulum: a pendulum that completes one vibration in two seconds (T = 2 s). With g = 9.8 m s⁻², ℓ = gT²/4π² ≈ 0.994 m.

On the Moon: T ∝ 1/√g. The value of g on the Moon is smaller, so a pendulum of the same length has a longer period there; it would not keep the same time.

book_ref.quote: The simple pendulum can be used to determine the gravitational acceleration at a particular location.

blocks.prompt: 10 A simple pendulum of length 0.90 m makes 20 complete vibrations in 38.2 s. Find the time period and the value of g at that place. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide the total time by the number of vibrations to get T, then use g = 4π²ℓ/T².

book_ref.quote: The time period T of the simple pendulum is measured using a stopwatch

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe how the shadow of a ball on a rotating turntable shows the link between S.H.M and uniform circular motion. Taking a particle P moving on a circle of radius x₀ with uniform angular velocity ω, derive the instantaneous displacement and instantaneous velocity of its projection Q, and find where the velocity is maximum. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Turntable: A ball is attached to the rim of a turntable of radius r. When the table rotates with constant angular speed ω, the ball moves in uniform circular motion. A beam of light casts its shadow on a screen; the shadow moves to and fro in S.H.M, like a body on a spring (Fig. 14.4). So the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter executes S.H.M.

Set-up: P moves on a circle of radius x₀ with uniform ω; its linear velocity vₚ = x₀ω is along the tangent. Q is the projection of P on the diameter; it oscillates about O.

Instantaneous displacement: If P starts at A, in time t the radius OP sweeps θ = ωt (Fig. 14.5). In triangle POQ:
OQ/OP = cos θ, i.e. x/x₀ = cos ωt
x = x₀ cos θ = x₀ cos ωt ... (14.11)

Instantaneous velocity: Q moves horizontally, so its velocity is the horizontal component of vₚ (Fig. 14.6):
v = vₚ cos(90° − θ) = vₚ sinθ
v = x₀ω sinθ = x₀ω sin ωt ... (14.12)
Using sinθ = √(1 − cos²θ) and cosθ = x/x₀:
v = x₀ω√(1 − x²/x₀²)
v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = √((k/m)(x₀² − x²)) ... (14.13)

Maximum velocity: At the mean position x = 0:
v_max = x₀ω = √(k/m) x₀ ... (14.14)
At the extreme positions x = ±x₀, v = 0.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, as Q vibrates horizontally, so instantaneous velocity of the point Q is horizontal component

blocks.prompt: 12 A body in S.H.M has amplitude 0.12 m and angular frequency 6 rad s⁻¹. Find (i) its maximum speed (ii) its speed when the displacement is 0.072 m. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Maximum speed is x₀ω at the mean position; at displacement x use v = ω√(x₀² − x²).

book_ref.quote: Eq. (14.13) should read v = ω√(x₀² − x²)

steps: x₀ = 0.12 m, ω = 6 rad s⁻¹, x = 0.072 m
blocks.final_answer: v_max = 0.72 m s⁻¹; v ≈ 0.576 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.072 m

blocks.prompt: 13 Derive the instantaneous acceleration of the projection of a particle moving on a circle with uniform angular velocity, and hence show that the projection executes S.H.M. Where is the acceleration maximum and where is it zero? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Let P move on a circle of radius x₀ with uniform angular velocity ω, and Q be its projection on the diameter at distance x from the centre O.

The acceleration aₚ of P is centripetal, directed towards the centre, with magnitude x₀ω² (Fig. 14.7). Its horizontal component lies along the diameter, so the acceleration of Q is the horizontal component of aₚ:
a = (aₚ)ₓ = aₚ cosθ
Taking the direction towards the centre (opposite to x) as negative, aₚ → −x₀ω², and cosθ = x/x₀:
a = −x₀ω²(x/x₀) = −ω²x
a = −xω² ... (14.15)
The negative sign shows that the acceleration is always directed towards the mean position.

As ω is constant, a ∝ −x. This is the mathematical condition of S.H.M: acceleration is directly proportional to displacement and directed towards the mean position. Hence the projection of a particle moving on a circle executes S.H.M.

Maximum and zero: |a| = ω²x is maximum (x₀ω²) at the extreme positions x = ±x₀, and zero at the mean position x = 0.

book_ref.quote: Thus, the acceleration of projection Q is equal to the horizontal component of aₚ.

blocks.prompt: 14 A particle moves on a circle of radius 0.25 m with a period of 2 s. Find the acceleration of its projection (i) when the projection is 0.10 m from the centre (ii) at an extreme position. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ω = 2π/T, then a = −ω²x; at an extreme x = x₀.

book_ref.quote: This expression is the mathematical condition of S.H.M

steps: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad s⁻¹, ω² = π² ≈ 9.87 s⁻²
At the extreme x = x₀ = 0.25 m: |a| = x₀ω² = 0.25 × 9.87 ≈ 2.47 m s⁻²
Both accelerations point towards the centre (mean position).
blocks.final_answer: (i) 0.987 m s⁻² towards the centre (ii) 2.47 m s⁻² towards the centre

blocks.prompt: 15 Define phase and phase constant. Using x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ), describe where the oscillating point is at t = 0, T/4, T/2, 3T/4 and T for φ = 0°, 90° and 180°. What is meant by oscillating in phase and out of phase? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Phase: the angle θ = ωt which specifies the displacement x as well as the direction of motion of a point executing S.H.M; it shows the state of motion of the oscillator. In general
x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ) ... (14.18)
The time-varying quantity (ωt + φ) is the phase of the motion. The constant φ is the phase constant (phase angle); its value depends on the displacement and velocity of the particle at t = 0. φ also gives the phase difference between the states of two oscillators.

Case φ = 0°: x = x₀ cos ωt (Fig. 14.8 a). At t = 0, T/2 and T (θ = 0, π, 2π) the point is at the extreme positions; at t = T/4 and 3T/4 (θ = π/2, 3π/2) it is at the mean position.

Case φ = 90°: x = x₀ cos(ωt + 90°) (Fig. 14.8 b). At t = 0, T/2 and T the point is at the mean position; at t = T/4 and 3T/4 it is at the extreme positions.

Case φ = 180°: x = x₀ cos(ωt + 180°) (Fig. 14.8 c). At t = 0 the point is at −x₀ (the opposite extreme), at T/4 and 3T/4 at the mean position, at T/2 at +x₀; the graph is the φ = 0° graph turned upside down.

In phase: phase difference 0° or 360°; the two systems move together.
Out of phase: phase difference 180°; when one is at +x₀ the other is at −x₀.

book_ref.quote: The quantity φ represents the phase difference between the states of motion of two oscillators.

blocks.prompt: 16 A body oscillates according to x = 0.1 cos ωt (x in metres) with a time period of 1.2 s. At t = 0.2 s find (i) its phase (ii) its displacement (iii) the magnitude of its velocity. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ω = 2π/T; the phase is ωt; then x = x₀ cos ωt and |v| = x₀ω sin ωt.

book_ref.quote: Where x is instantaneous displacement, x₀ is maximum displacement

blocks.prompt: 17 Write the expressions for the displacement, velocity and acceleration of a body executing S.H.M starting from an extreme position, and describe their graphs against time. State where each is maximum and zero, and give the phase differences between them. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Displacement:
x = x₀ cos ωt ... (14.19)
Graph (Fig. 14.9 a) is a cosine curve starting at +x₀. Displacement is maximum (x₀) at the extreme positions and zero at the mean position.

(ii) Velocity: magnitude
v = x₀ω sin ωt ... (14.20)
With its sign, for x = x₀ cos ωt, v = −x₀ω sin ωt, so the velocity graph starts at zero and falls first (Fig. 14.9 b). Velocity is maximum (x₀ω) at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions.

(iii) Acceleration: a = −ω²x; putting x = x₀ cos ωt,
a = −x₀ω² cos ωt ... (14.21)
Graph (Fig. 14.9 c) starts at −x₀ω², a mirror image of the displacement graph. Acceleration is maximum (x₀ω²) at the extreme positions and zero at the mean position.

Phase differences:
• Velocity and displacement: π/2.
• Velocity and acceleration: π/2.
• Acceleration and displacement: π, since a = −ω²x makes them always opposite.

book_ref.quote: The graphical representations of displacement, velocity and acceleration of a body executing SHM

blocks.prompt: 18 A body executes S.H.M according to x = x₀ cos ωt with x₀ = 0.05 m and ω = 8 rad s⁻¹. Find its displacement, velocity and acceleration at t = 0.1 s (angle in radians). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ωt in radians; then x = x₀ cos ωt, v = −x₀ω sin ωt, a = −ω²x.

book_ref.quote: The acceleration of the particle executing SHM is given by the expression:

blocks.final_answer: x ≈ 0.0348 m, v ≈ −0.287 m s⁻¹ (moving towards the mean position), a ≈ −2.23 m s⁻²

blocks.prompt: 19 Using the average restoring force, find the work done in stretching a spring to its amplitude and hence the elastic potential energy of a mass-spring oscillator. Derive its kinetic energy at displacement x and prove that its total energy is constant. Express the total energy in terms of m and ω, and describe the energy graph. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Average force: The restoring force is zero at x = 0 and F = kx₀ at x = x₀, so
F_av = (0 + kx₀)/2 = ½kx₀
Work done in stretching to x₀:
W = F_av × x₀ = ½kx₀(x₀) = ½kx₀²
This work is stored as elastic potential energy. At any displacement x:
(P.E.)inst = ½kx² ... (14.22)
It is zero at x = 0 and maximum at x = ±x₀:
(P.E.)max = ½kx₀² ... (14.23)

Kinetic energy: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) with ω = √(k/m):
v = √((k/m)(x₀² − x²)) ... (14.24)
v_max = √(k/m) x₀ at x = 0 ... (14.25)
K.E. = ½mv² = ½k(x₀² − x²) ... (14.26)
At the mean position P.E. = 0 and the energy is entirely kinetic:
T.E = K.E.max = ½mv²max = ½kx₀² ... (14.27)

Total energy at x:
T.E = K.E + P.E = ½k(x₀² − x²) + ½kx² = ½kx₀² ... (14.28)
This does not depend on x, so the total energy is constant and directly proportional to the square of the amplitude. With k = mω²:
T.E = ½mω²x₀²

Graph (Fig. 14.11): plotted against x from −x₀ to +x₀, P.E. is a parabola zero at the centre, K.E. an inverted parabola maximum at the centre, and T.E a horizontal line. Energy changes between K.E. and P.E. but their sum stays constant.

book_ref.quote: Thus, average value of force from the mean position to the extreme position is:

blocks.prompt: 20 A 0.4 kg mass on a spring of constant 160 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 5 cm. At x = 3 cm find its potential energy, kinetic energy and speed, and check that the total energy equals ½kx₀². (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: P.E. = ½kx², K.E. = ½k(x₀² − x²); the speed follows from K.E. = ½mv².

book_ref.quote: The total energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy of the system at displacement

blocks.prompt: 21 Explain free oscillations, forced oscillations and damped oscillations with examples. Describe light, heavy and critical damping, and explain why shock absorbers are used in a car. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Free oscillations: A body executes free vibrations when it oscillates with its natural frequency without the interference of an external force. Example: a simple pendulum slightly displaced vibrates freely with a natural frequency depending only on its length (Fig. 14.12). With no resistive force the total energy, and so the amplitude, remains constant.

Forced oscillations: If a freely oscillating system is subjected to an external force, forced vibrations take place. Examples: a swing struck repeatedly (Fig. 14.13); a factory floor vibrating due to heavy machinery; the sounding wooden boards of string instruments.

Damped oscillations: In practice, dissipating forces such as air resistance and friction act. The oscillations with decreasing amplitude in the presence of resistive forces are damped oscillations, and the resistive forces are damping forces. Example: a girl on a swing oscillates with smaller and smaller amplitude and eventually stops (Figs. 14.14, 14.15); touching a vibrating tuning fork.

Types of damping:
• Light damping: reduces energy and amplitude gradually, e.g. a playground swing.
• Heavy damping: takes a longer time before the body comes to rest, e.g. a pendulum in thick oil.
• Critical damping: the object returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time, e.g. car shock absorbers.

Shock absorbers: On a bumpy, rough road the car's suspension would oscillate excessively. Shock absorbers damp these oscillations (Fig. 14.16), ensuring a comfortable ride for the passengers.

book_ref.quote: In an ideal free oscillation system, we have studied that the total mechanical energy

blocks.prompt: 22 A simple pendulum of length 0.62 m is slightly displaced and left to vibrate freely (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Find its natural frequency and the number of free vibrations it makes in one minute. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: A free pendulum vibrates at its natural frequency f = (1/2π)√(g/ℓ); multiply by 60 s.

book_ref.quote: For example, a simple pendulum shown in Fig. 14.12 vibrates freely with its natural frequency

steps: Vibrations in 60 s: n = f × t = 0.633 × 60 ≈ 38
blocks.final_answer: f ≈ 0.633 Hz; about 38 vibrations per minute

blocks.prompt: 23 What is resonance? Describe an experiment with pendulums of different lengths hung from a horizontal rod to demonstrate it. Explain how resonance is used in a microwave oven and in tuning a radio, and why soldiers break step on a bridge. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Forced oscillation: A damped oscillator can keep a constant amplitude if a periodic external (driving) force acts on it; its frequency is the driving frequency. The amplitude depends on the relation between the driving frequency and the natural frequency.

Resonance: If the frequency of the driving force is the same as the natural frequency of the body, the amplitude of vibration is very much increased. This is resonance.

Experiment (Fig. 14.17): Pendulums A and B (length ℓ₁) and C and D (length ℓ₂) hang from a horizontal rod. Another pendulum P, whose length can be ℓ₁ or ℓ₂, is also hung. With P of length ℓ₁ set swinging, its vibration reaches the others through the rod. A and B, having the same length and so the same natural frequency as P, start vibrating with growing amplitude: resonance. C and D, with a different natural frequency, remain almost at rest. With P of length ℓ₂, C and D resonate while A and B remain at rest.

Microwave oven: microwaves of about 2.45 GHz (wavelength about 12 cm) excite water molecules in food; they oscillate at the same frequency and collide, and friction turns their kinetic energy into heat. Containers without water do not heat up.

Radio tuning: turning the knob changes the natural frequency of the receiver circuit. When it equals the transmission frequency of a station, resonance occurs and the receiver absorbs maximum energy from that station's signal, so only that station is heard.

Bridge: soldiers marching in step might match the natural frequency of the bridge; resonance could make the bridge vibrate with large amplitude and collapse, so they break step.

book_ref.quote: To demonstrate the resonance phenomenon, we perform a simple experiment.

blocks.prompt: 24 A playground swing behaves like a simple pendulum of length 2.5 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). At what frequency, and at what time interval, should it be pushed so that its amplitude builds up by resonance? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For resonance the push frequency must equal the swing's natural frequency, found from the pendulum formula.

book_ref.quote: It must be noted that natural frequency of swing matches the frequency of pushes

steps: Resonance needs the pushes at the natural frequency: one push every 3.17 s (0.315 Hz).
blocks.final_answer: Push at about 0.315 Hz, i.e. once every 3.17 s

blocks.prompt: 25 Explain the relationship between resonance and standing waves with the help of (i) the Rubens tube (ii) the Chladni plate (iii) acoustic levitation. How does damping affect the sharpness of resonance? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Rubens tube: a metal pipe with holes drilled along its top, sealed at both ends; one end is attached to a small speaker or frequency generator and the other to a supply of flammable gas, which leaks from the holes and burns (Fig. 14.21). When sound of a resonance frequency is produced, a standing wave forms inside the tube with points of higher and lower pressure. More gas escapes where the pressure is high (tall flames) and less where it is low (low flames). Tall flames stand at every pressure antinode, half a wavelength apart, so the flames reveal the nodes and antinodes.

(ii) Chladni plate: a circular or square metal plate fixed horizontally to a vibrator and driven at its centre. At the frequency of a resonant normal mode, nodes and antinodes form over its surface. The plate does not vibrate at the nodes; sand sprinkled on it shifts from the antinodes to the stationary nodes and shows the standing-wave pattern (Fig. 14.22).

(iii) Acoustic levitation: suspends small particles (bits of styrofoam, water droplets) in air against gravity using radiation pressure of high-intensity ultrasonic waves. A transducer sends sound to a reflector; incident and reflected waves form a standing wave with minimum pressure at the nodes and maximum at the antinodes. This pressure difference pushes particles against gravity and traps them at the nodes, which act as acoustic traps (Fig. 14.23).

Sharpness of resonance: the resonant amplitude and its sharpness both depend on damping. The smaller the damping, the greater the amplitude and the sharper the resonance; a heavily damped system has a fairly flat resonance curve (Fig. 14.20). For example, a lead bob resonates with a much greater amplitude than a pith ball of equal size, because air resistance damps the pith ball much more.

book_ref.quote: There is relationship between standing wave and resonance phenomenon

blocks.prompt: 26 In a Rubens tube, adjacent tall flames are 17 cm apart. Taking the speed of sound in the gas as 340 m s⁻¹ and using frequency = speed/wavelength, find the wavelength and the frequency of the sound. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Adjacent tall flames (pressure antinodes) are half a wavelength apart, so double the spacing to get λ.

book_ref.quote: Tall flames stand at every pressure antinode, crests and troughs alike, half a wavelength apart

steps: Spacing of tall flames = λ/2 = 0.17 m
